'''thirstless''' (thėrst′les), ''a.'' [< ''thirst'' + ''-less.''] Having no thirst. {{smaller block|Thus as it falls out among men of ''thirstless'' minds in their fortunes. {{right|''Bp. Reynolds'', On the Passions, p. 502. (''Latham.'')}}}} '''thirstlew†''', ''a.'' [ME. ''thurstlew''; < ''thirst'' + ''-lew'' as in ''drunkelew.''] Thirsty. ''Lydgate'', Minor Poems, p. 75. '''thirsty''' (thėrs′ti), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. and dial. also ''thristy''; < ME. ''thursti'', ''thresti'', ''thristi'', < AS. ''thurstig'', ''thrystig'' = OFries. ''dorstig'', ''torstig'' = D. ''dorstig'' = MLG. ''dorstich'', LG. ''dorstig'' = OHG. ''durstag'', MHG. ''durstec'', G. ''durstig'' = Sw. Dan. ''törstig'' (cf. Icel. ''thyrstr''), thirsty; as ''thirst'' + ''-y''1.] 1. Feeling thirst; suffering for want of drink. {{smaller block|As cold waters to a ''thirsty'' soul, so is good news from a far country. {{right|Prov. xxv. 25.}}}} {{smaller block|What streams the verdant succory supply,
And how the ''thirsty'' plant drinks rivers dry. {{right|''Addison'', tr. of Virgil's Georgics, iv.}}}} 2. Dry; parched; arid. {{smaller block|The parched ground shall become a pool, and the ''thirsty'' land springs of water. {{right|Isa. xxxv. 7.}}}} {{smaller block|The word "desert" is used, in the West, to describe alike lands in which the principle of life, if it ever existed, is totally extinct, and those other lands which are merely ''thirsty.'' {{right|''The Century'', XXXVIII. 298.}}}}

3. Vehemently desirous; craving: with ''after'', ''for'', etc.

{{smaller block|To be ''thirsty after'' tottering honour.
{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, iii. 2. 40.}}}}

4†. Sharp; eager; active.

{{smaller block|We've been ''thirsty''
In our pursuit.
{{right|''Ford'', Fancies, i. 1.}}}}

5. Causing thirst. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Our natures do pursue,
Like rats that ravin down their proper bane,
A ''thirsty'' evil; and when we drink we die.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 2. 134.}}}}

'''thirteen''' (thėr′tēn′), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Also dial. ''thretteen''; < ME. ''thrittene'', ''threttene'', ''threottene'', < AS. ''threótȳne'' = OFries. ''threttene'' = D. ''dertien'' = MLG. ''druttein'', LG. ''dartein'' = OHG. ''drizēn'', MHG. ''drīzehen'', ''drīzēn'', G. ''dreizehn'' = Icel. ''threttān'' = Sw. ''tretton'' = Dan. ''tretten'' = Goth. *''threistaihun'' = L. ''tredecim'' (> It. ''tredeci'' = Pg. ''treze'' = Sp. ''trece'' = F. ''treize'') = Gr. τρεισ(καί)δεκα = Skt. ''trayodaça'', thirteen; as ''three'' + ''ten''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Being three more than ten; consisting of one more than twelve: a cardinal numeral.

'''II.''' ''n.'' 1. The number which consists of the sum of twelve and one, or of ten and three.—2. A symbol representing thirteen units, as 13, XIII, or xiii.—3. A silver shilling worth 13 pence, current in Ireland during the early part of the nineteenth century.

{{smaller block|F. A. M. is doubtless chronologically correct as to the shilling in Ireland having been worth thirteen pence previous to 1825-6, but colloquially it continued to be called a ''thirteen'' to a considerably later period—so late as 1835 to my knowledge.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., I. 77.}}}}

A feeling of dryness in the mouth and throat; the uncomfortable sensations arising from the want of fluid nutriment; the uneasiness or suffering occasioned by want of drink; vehement desire for drink. {{smaller|The sensations of thirst are chiefly referred to the thorax and fauces, but the condition is really one affecting the entire body. The excessive pains of thirst compared with those of hunger are due to the fact that the deprivation of liquids is a condition with which all the tissues sympathize. Every solid and every fluid of the body contains water, and hence abstraction or diminution of the watery constituents is followed by a general depression of the whole system. Thirst is a common symptom of febrile and other diseases. Death from thirst, as of persons in a desert, appears to be invariably preceded by acute mania.}} {{smaller block|Than he commanded him to Presoun, and alle his Tresoure aboute him; and so he dyed for Hungre and ''Threst.'' {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 230.}}}} {{smaller block|Raymounde tho lepte vp hys coursere vppon, To the fantain and wel of ''thrust'' gan to go. {{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. ''se'', etc., the (but by some identified with the impv. (AS. ''seó'', OHG. ''sē'', Goth. ''sai'') of the verb ''see''1). The pl. of ''this'' appears in two forms, ''these'' (< ME. That is now present or at hand: a demonstrative adjective used to point out with particularity a person or thing that is present in place or in thought. {{smaller|It denotes—(''a'') Some person or thing that is present or near in place or time, or is nearer in place or time than some other person or thing, or has just been mentioned or referred to, and is therefore opposed to or the correlative of ''that'': as, ''this'' city was founded five hundred years ago, or one hundred years earlier than ''that'' (city); ''this'' day; ''this'' time of night; ''these'' words.}} {{smaller block|Of ''theise'' three Greynes sprong a Tree, as the Aungelle seyde that it scholde, and bere a Fruyt thorghe the whiche Fruyt Adam scholde be saved. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 12.}}}} {{smaller block|Frote youre visage with ''this'' herbe, and youre handes. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 76.}}}} {{smaller block|In ''thys'' cite I abode Tewysday, all day and all nyght. {{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 5.}}}}
